topic: N-gram Language Models, Smoothing, and Perplexity

questions.question: In the formula for Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) of a bigram P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁), the numerator is the count of the bigram C(wᵢ₋₁, wᵢ). What is the denominator?

options.A: The count of the unigram C(wᵢ).
options.B: The total number of tokens N.
options.C: The count of the unigram C(wᵢ₋₁).

questions.reasoning: MLE for bigrams is calculated as C(wᵢ₋₁, wᵢ) / C(wᵢ₋₁).

questions.question: What mathematical concept is used to transform the product of probabilities P(p₁ × p₂ × ...) in language modeling into a sum of log probabilities (log(p₁) + log(p₂) + ...)?
questions.reasoning: Log space calculation converts products to sums, preventing numerical underflow.

questions.question: Why is using Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing generally avoided for large N-gram models in practical NLP applications?

options.A: It is computationally slower than MLE.
options.B: It fails to eliminate zero counts.
options.C: It drastically changes the original probability distribution (a "blunt instrument").
options.D: It leads to the vanishing gradient problem.

questions.reasoning: Add-1 smoothing significantly distorts probability distributions in large vocabularies.

questions.question: In the context of N-gram language models, what is the core issue that smoothing techniques are designed to address?

options.A: Overfitting on training data that leads to zero probabilities for unseen sequences in the test set.
options.B: Underfitting the training data due to Markov assumptions.
options.D: The calculation of the Cross-Entropy Loss.

questions.reasoning: Smoothing addresses the zero probability problem for unseen N-grams.

questions.question: How does the Bigram model (N=2) approximate the true probability P(wᵢ | w₁...wᵢ₋₁)?
questions.reasoning: Bigram models use only the immediately preceding word: P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁).

questions.question: If a sentence contains an N-gram that has a raw count of zero in the training data, what is the resulting joint probability of that entire sentence if no smoothing is applied?
questions.reasoning: Any zero probability in the product makes the entire joint probability zero.

questions.question: If Model A has a perplexity of 20 and Model B has a perplexity of 10, which statement is generally true about their performance on the test set?

options.A: Model A assigns a higher probability to the test set.
options.B: Model B is the better model, assigning a higher probability to the test set.
options.C: Perplexity cannot be compared across different model sizes.
options.D: Both models are performing equally well.

questions.reasoning: Lower perplexity indicates better model performance (higher probability assigned to test set).

questions.question: In a language model, what does the perplexity metric PP(W) represent mathematically?

options.A: The average negative log-likelihood of the sequence.
options.B: The inverse probability of the test set, normalized by the number of words.
options.C: The total number of unique words in the vocabulary.
options.D: The geometric mean of all word probabilities.

questions.reasoning: Perplexity is the inverse probability normalized by sequence length.

questions.question: The smoothing technique known as "Interpolation" combines probability estimates from which sources?

options.A: Probability estimates from different contexts (unigram, bigram, trigram, etc.).
options.B: Only the unigram distribution and the vocabulary size.
options.D: Only the counts of words appearing more than 5 times.

questions.reasoning: Interpolation combines multiple N-gram models (unigram, bigram, trigram, etc.).

questions.question: An N-gram language model uses the Chain Rule of Probability and applies the Markov Assumption. How does the Markov Assumption simplify the conditional probability P(wᵢ | w₁...wᵢ₋₁) for a bigram model?

options.D: It simplifies to P(wᵢ | w₁, w₂).

questions.reasoning: The Markov assumption for bigrams assumes only the immediately preceding word matters.

questions.question: An N-gram that has never appeared in the training data is said to have a:
questions.reasoning: Unseen N-grams have a count of zero in the training corpus.

questions.question: In a corpus, the phrase "want to" appears 608 times, and the word "want" appears 927 times. What is the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) for P(to | want)?
questions.reasoning: MLE is calculated as C(want, to) / C(want) = 608 / 927.

questions.question: Given a vocabulary size V, what is the formula for the Add-1 (Laplace) smoothed estimate of a bigram P*(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁)?
questions.reasoning: Add-1 smoothing adds 1 to the numerator and V to the denominator.

questions.question: If a trigram is assigned a zero count in a language model, the backoff smoothing approach suggests using the model's estimate for which lower-order model next?
questions.reasoning: Backoff moves from trigram to bigram to unigram sequentially.

questions.question: In evaluating a language model, minimizing perplexity is mathematically equivalent to achieving what goal?

options.B: Minimizing the size of the test set.
options.C: Maximizing the probability of the unseen test set.

questions.reasoning: Lower perplexity equals higher probability assigned to the test set.

questions.question: If Model A achieves a perplexity of 50 and Model B achieves a perplexity of 100 on the same test corpus, which statement is true?

options.A: Model B is better because higher perplexity means better generalization.
options.B: Model A is better because lower perplexity means better prediction.
options.C: Model A is more complex than Model B.
options.D: Model B is less prone to the zero count problem.

questions.reasoning: Lower perplexity indicates better model performance.
